historicalReferences: Doohan's epic battles with Crivillé at the Dry Sack corner are legendary here – a testament to the circuit's demanding nature.
Remember Valentino Rossi's incredible comeback win in 2003? A true masterclass of race craft at Jerez.
This is the track where Jorge Lorenzo cemented his status as a MotoGP icon, dominating here for years.
The 1996 European Grand Prix saw Michael Schumacher take a dominant victory, showcasing his wet-weather prowess.
In 2013, the infamous clash between Marquez and Lorenzo at the final corner is still talked about today.
Jerez has seen countless championship deciders, each adding to the track's rich history and legacy.
Who can forget the nail-biting finish in 2005 when Rossi and Gibernau went wheel-to-wheel to the line?
This circuit has been a proving ground for generations of racing legends. The names echo through the stands.
The 1986 Spanish Grand Prix, with Ayrton Senna taking the win after a thrilling race-long battle is a memorable moment.
Many great careers have been launched here at Jerez. It remains an important stop on the racing calendar.
cornerCallouts: The riders need to be precise through Turn 1, Expo '92, setting themselves up for the long right-hander that follows.
Negotiating Curva Michelin requires absolute commitment and precision – get it wrong, and you'll be punished.
The braking zone for Dry Sack is crucial; it's a prime overtaking opportunity.
The riders will be fighting the front end into Curva Sito Pons, trying to maintain their line.
The exit of Curva Sito Pons is critical for setting up the run down to the hairpin at Curva Lorenzo.
The long right-hander, Curva Ferrari, really tests the rider's physical endurance.
The fast chicane through Turn 11 and 12, Curva Ducados and Curva Nieto, requires a delicate balance of aggression and control.
Heading into the final corner, Curva Peluqui, the riders will be looking to make a last-gasp overtake.
strategyPoints: Tire management is absolutely crucial around this 4.218km layout. The abrasive surface will punish aggressive riding.
A one-stop strategy is likely the fastest, but the pit window is relatively short, requiring pinpoint accuracy from the team.
Fuel consumption will be a factor, particularly for riders pushing hard in the early stages.
The afternoon heat will only exacerbate tire degradation, forcing riders to adapt their strategies on the fly.
With a relatively short lap, traffic management will be key, especially in the final stages of the race.
The length of the pit lane here at Jerez adds valuable seconds to the pit stop time, so every millisecond counts.
The long right-handers will put immense stress on the left side of the tires, which could influence tire choice.
Considering the layout, expect to see teams experimenting with different gear ratios to optimize acceleration out of the corners.
weatherCommentary: The Andalusian sun is beating down, creating ideal racing conditions. Clear skies as far as the eye can see.
The wind could be a factor today, particularly on the back straight. Expect to see some riders struggling with stability.
The track temperature is soaring, which could lead to increased tire degradation. A real test for the teams and riders.
There's a slight breeze coming in off the Atlantic, which may help to cool the track slightly, but it's still going to be hot out there.
The humidity is relatively low, which will help with rider comfort, but tire wear remains a major concern in these conditions.
